sessions.title: Welcome: the road to Emmaus
sessions.summary: Every journey of faith starts with Jesus walking beside us, often before we recognize him.
lesson: On the first Easter Sunday, two disciples walked home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were sad and confused: Jesus had died, and they did not understand the news that he was alive.

A stranger joined them on the road. He listened to them, then explained the Scriptures, showing how everything pointed to Jesus. When they reached the village they begged him, "Stay with us." At supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened: it was Jesus.

Later they said to each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?" That is the heart of this journey. You will hear the Scriptures, ask questions, walk with others, and come to the table of the Eucharist. Jesus is already walking with you, even on the days you do not see him.
You do not need to have everything figured out. The disciples on the road were full of doubts. Bring your questions; that is what this time is for.
sessions.reflection: What brought you to begin this journey? What are you hoping to find?

sessions.title: Prayer: talking with God
sessions.summary: Prayer is simply a conversation with God who loves you. Anyone can start today.
lesson: Prayer is lifting your heart and mind to God. It does not need special words; you can talk to God as you would to someone who loves you. Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called prayer "a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven."

Catholics pray in many ways: in our own words, with traditional prayers like the Our Father, with the Bible, in silence, and together at Mass. Traditional prayers are helpful when we do not know what to say; they have been prayed by millions of people before us.
When the disciples asked Jesus, "Lord, teach us to pray," he gave them the Our Father. It is the perfect place to start. Try praying it slowly once a day this week, thinking about each line.

A simple daily habit: when you wake up, make the Sign of the Cross and offer your day to God. Before sleep, think back over the day, thank God for one good thing, and say sorry for anything you regret.
sessions.reflection: What would help you make a few minutes of prayer part of your day?

sessions.title: The journey of faith: the Trinity, faith, and the God who is love
sessions.summary: God made us out of love, to share his life. He has shown us who he is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

sources.title: Psalm 23 in the modern translation from your class sheet (US bishops)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 1
lesson: This session opens with Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd," next to a picture of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Both say the same thing: we are not walking alone. God goes ahead of us, walks beside us, and leads us home.
## Psalm 23

> The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing.
He hath set me in a place of pasture.
He hath brought me up, on the water of refreshment: he hath converted my soul.
He hath led me on the paths of justice, for his own name's sake.
For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me.
Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me.
Thou hast prepared a table before me against them that afflict me.
Thou hast anointed my head with oil; and my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it!
And thy mercy will follow me all the days of my life.
And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord unto length of days. — Psalm 23 (22), Douay-Rheims

Your class sheet uses a modern translation that is under copyright, so the psalm is printed here in the Douay-Rheims, the classic Catholic English Bible, which anyone may share. The modern wording from your sheet ("there is nothing I lack… goodness and mercy will pursue me… for endless days") is one tap away under Sources.
[[art:Angelsatmamre-trinity-rublev-1410.jpg|Andrei Rublev, The Trinity (about 1410): the three visitors to Abraham, an image of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit]]
## Made by love, for love

God is infinitely perfect and blessed in himself. He did not make us to add to his own happiness. He chose freely, out of his own love and goodness, to create us so that we could share his blessed life (Catechism 1, 293).
We were made by the God who is love, and we are made for his love (Catechism 27-30).
> Our hearts are restless until they rest in you. — St. Augustine
At every moment of our lives God draws near to us, calling us to seek him, to know him and to love him (Catechism 1). Like the shepherd of Psalm 23, he is the one who comes looking for us.
## One God, three Persons
There is only one God (Catechism 200-202). Yet this one God has revealed himself as a communion of three Persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 221).
By sending us the Son and the Holy Spirit, God has shown us his "innermost secret": his very being is a communion of love.
> God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and he has destined us to share in that exchange. — Catechism 221
Your drawing of the Trinity: the Father is God, Jesus is God, the Holy Spirit is God. But the Father is not Jesus, Jesus is not the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father.
[[figure:trinity]]
The Holy Trinity is three Persons in one God. It is not three gods, and it is not one God wearing three masks.

> We worship one God in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity, without either confusing the persons or dividing the substance; for the person of the Father is one, the Son's is another and the Holy Spirit's another; but the Godhead of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal, their majesty coeternal. — Catechism 266
## What faith is
Faith is our response to the God who has made himself known to us. It has two sides (Catechism 150):
- Intellect (believing): with our minds we say yes to everything God has revealed.
- Will (entrusting ourselves): with our hearts we hold on to God personally and entrust our lives to him.
[[figure:faith]]
Faith is not only agreeing with ideas, and it is not only a feeling. It is both: believing who God is, and entrusting ourselves to him.
## Three key elements of prayer
1. Praise: focus on God. This is "the truth zone": God is in control, he loves us, and we show him our love.
2. Petitions: ask for our needs.
3. Ask his forgiveness: we have sinned, and we also choose to forgive others.

> We must speak to God as a friend speaks to his friend, servant to his master; now asking some favor, now acknowledging our faults, and communicating to him all that concerns us, our thoughts, our fears, our projects, our desires, and in all things seeking his counsel. — St. Ignatius of Loyola
sessions.reflection: Pray Psalm 23 slowly this week. Where in your life do you need to trust that God is the shepherd walking with you?

deeper.title: Why two creeds?
deeper.text:
A creed is a short summary of what Christians believe. The Church keeps two from the early centuries, and both proclaim faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Apostles' Creed is one of the earliest, first used in Rome when people were baptized. We still use it at Baptisms and to begin the Rosary.

The Nicene Creed was first written at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD to answer questions that had arisen about the Trinity and about whether Jesus is truly God. Its extra detail is about clarity. It is the creed we normally say at Sunday Mass and on major feasts.

sessions.title: Divine Revelation: God seeking us
sessions.summary: God has shown us who he is and his loving plan to save us. It reaches us through Scripture, Tradition and the Church's teaching, all three together.

sources.title: Matthew 16:13-19, the keys of the kingdom
John 16:12-15, the Spirit will guide you into all truth
Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation)
Catechism 50-100: God comes to meet us

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 2
lesson: Your Lesson 2 sheet opens with Perugino's painting in the Sistine Chapel, and you labelled it: Jesus, the key to the kingdom, and Peter, the first pope (Matthew 16:18-19). Hold on to that picture. It shows how God makes sure what he revealed is handed on faithfully.
[[art:Entrega de las llaves a San Pedro (Perugino).jpg|Perugino, The Delivery of the Keys (1481-82), Sistine Chapel: Jesus hands Peter, the first pope, the keys to the kingdom]]
## The five main points
1. Divine Revelation: God revealed himself and his loving plan for humanity, for our salvation.
2. Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of God's revelation.
3. Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture are the oral and the written handing on of the faith.
4. The Deposit of Faith has been entrusted to the teaching Magisterium of the Church, which has authority as the interpreter of Scripture and Tradition.
5. We need all three, Sacred Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium. One cannot stand without the other two.
## Hear the word and do it

> But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if a man be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he shall be compared to a man beholding his own countenance in a glass. For he beheld himself, and went his way, and presently forgot what manner of man he was. But he that hath looked into the perfect law of liberty, and hath continued therein, not becoming a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work; this man shall be blessed in his deed. — James 1:22-25, Douay-Rheims
(Your sheet labels this passage "1 Peter 22-25"; it is actually James 1:22-25. Your sheet uses a modern translation that is under copyright, so it is printed here in the Douay-Rheims.)

Freedom is not doing whatever you want, but doing what you ought to do. If God is a loving Father, he knows what is best for us. Through Divine Revelation the Catholic Church has been given the tools to help us live in true freedom. The final goal is for us to share eternal life one day with God and our heavenly family. We are not alone: the Church on earth and in heaven helps us on our journey through life.
## Scripture, Tradition and the Church together

> Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the teaching authority of the Church, in accord with God's most wise design, are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without the others, and all together and each in its own way under the action of the one Holy Spirit contribute effectively to the salvation of souls. — Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum 10

Sacred Tradition is the handing on, through the apostles' preaching and witness, of everything Christ did and taught, carried in the Church's teaching, life and worship (Catechism 76). The Bible is the part of Divine Revelation that the Holy Spirit chose to have written down. The fullness of truth is found in Scripture and Tradition together. So nothing in Sacred Tradition can contradict Sacred Scripture, and Scripture is understood and interpreted in the light of Tradition.
Your drawing: a stool with the Church as the seat, and Scripture, the Magisterium and Tradition as the three legs.
[[figure:stool]]
## Key points from the workbook
- God's plan: God chose to show himself and his loving plan of salvation so that we can know him and love him (Catechism 50-52).

- Step by step: he made himself known gradually, by deeds and words, through salvation history. It reaches its peak in Jesus Christ, the Son of God made man, who is the fullness of Revelation (Catechism 53-65).
- Two ways of handing on: what Jesus revealed was passed on in the Church by word of mouth, through Sacred Tradition, and in writing, through Sacred Scripture (Catechism 75-79).
- The deposit of faith: the apostles entrusted this treasure, held in Scripture and Tradition, to the Church's teaching office, the Magisterium, to interpret it faithfully (Catechism 84-85).

- All three: to know and understand God's revelation, a Christian needs Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the Magisterium. They are so connected that one cannot stand without the others (Catechism 95).
## Complete, and still unfolding

Your sheet includes a reflection from Mark Mallett's book The Final Confrontation. In my own words, his point is this: nothing new needs to be added to Divine Revelation. God has said everything in his Son, Jesus Christ, who entrusted it all to the apostles. You could say Christ gave them the whole "bud" of Revelation, and over the centuries it keeps opening. Jesus promised as much:

> I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth. For he shall not speak of himself; but what things soever he shall hear, he shall speak; and the things that are to come, he shall shew you. — John 16:12-13, Douay-Rheims
With the death of the last apostle, Christ had given the whole of Revelation to the Church. Yet the Church keeps understanding it more deeply:

> Yet even if Revelation is already complete, it has not been made completely explicit; it remains for Christian faith gradually to grasp its full significance over the course of the centuries. — Catechism 66

Mallett compares this to the petals of the bud opening one by one, each bringing more light and understanding to the Church. He believes they are still opening, and will keep opening for all eternity, as we discover more and more of the infinite wisdom and beauty of God.

deeper.title: Your two question marks: salvation history and Magisterium
deeper.text:
Salvation history is the story of everything God has done to rescue humanity and draw us back to himself: from creation, through Abraham, Moses and the prophets, to Jesus, and on through the Church until he comes again. The Bible is, at heart, this one long story.

Magisterium (from the Latin for "teacher") is the Church's teaching office: the pope and the bishops united with him, the successors of Peter and the apostles. When it teaches on faith and morals, it guards and explains what God has already revealed in Scripture and Tradition. It serves the word of God; it never invents something new.

sessions.reflection: Is there a part of God's word you have heard but not yet put into practice? What is one small step you could take this week?

sessions.title: The Bible: God's love letter
sessions.summary: The Bible is God's love letter to his children: inspired by the Holy Spirit, read with the Church, and meant to be prayed.
sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 3
lesson: [[art:Saint Jerome Writing-Caravaggio (1605-6).jpg|Caravaggio, Saint Jerome Writing (about 1606): Jerome translated the Bible into Latin]]
## The Bible is God's loving communication with each of us

Your sheet quotes Dr. Scott Hahn's book A Father Who Keeps His Promises. In my own words, he says: Scripture is one of the most precious heirlooms in our family. It records the high points of a divine drama. It is not a dry, impersonal history lesson but a passionate love story: the astonishing story of a God who came to seek and save the lost, at enormous cost to himself.

Hahn adds that we often read Bible stories like simple morality tales, where the hero in the white hat beats the villain in the black hat and rides off into the sunset. But God inspired Scripture to teach us something much deeper. The Bible is a long love letter from the Father to his beloved children, who are still on their earthly pilgrimage.
## The Bible is inspired by the Holy Spirit
1. Sacred Scripture contains the Word of God in the words of men (Catechism 101).

2. God is the author of Sacred Scripture. He inspired human writers who wrote as true authors, using their own language, style and abilities. But God worked in them and through them, so that they wrote "whatever he wanted written, and no more" (Catechism 105-106).
3. Because God is the divine author, everything the human writers affirm is affirmed by the Holy Spirit, so the Scriptures always teach the truth (Catechism 107).
## The Catholic approach to interpreting Scripture correctly
1. The Bible is not read in a literalistic way, but literarily: paying attention to what the human writers meant to say, and to what God wants to reveal through them (Catechism 108-114).

2. To discover what the sacred authors intended, the reader must consider the conditions of their time and culture, the kinds of writing used then, and the ways people felt, spoke and told stories. The truth is presented in history, in prophecy, in poetry and in other kinds of writing (Catechism 110).
3. According to an ancient tradition, there are two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, and the spiritual sense is divided into three (Catechism 115).
- The literal sense: the meaning carried by the words of Scripture, found through careful study and explanation of the text (exegesis). All the other senses are built on the literal.
- The spiritual sense: because God's plan is one, not only the words of Scripture but also the real things and events it speaks about can be signs.
The three parts of the spiritual sense:
1. The allegorical sense: we understand the events in the Bible more deeply by seeing what they mean in Christ. For example, the crossing of the Red Sea is a sign of Baptism.
2. The moral sense: the events in Scripture should lead us to act justly. As St. Paul said, they were written "for our instruction" (1 Corinthians 10:11).
3. The anagogical sense (meaning "leading"): we see events and realities in light of their eternal meaning. Jerusalem, for example, points to the heavenly city (Catechism 115-118).
To put it more simply:
> The Letter speaks of deeds; Allegory to faith; The Moral how to act; Anagogy our destiny. — Catechism 118
## How the Church discerns which books are part of the Bible (the canon of Scripture)

1. All Scripture tells a single story: the story of salvation that reaches its high point in Jesus. The Old Testament prepares for the New, and the New Testament fulfills the Old (Catechism 101-102, 122, 128-129).
2. The Catholic Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, has discerned which books belong in the list (or canon) of authentic Scriptures (Catechism 120).
3. This discernment took place through the apostolic Tradition of the Church.
4. The completed list of these books is called the canon of Scripture. There are 46 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament.
[[figure:canon]]
## The canon of the Catholic Bible
The Old Testament (Hebrew Scriptures):
- The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy.
- Historical books: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Tobit, Judith, Esther, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees.
- Wisdom books: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, Sirach.
- The Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Baruch, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi.
The New Testament (Christian Scriptures):
- Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John.
- Historical: Acts of the Apostles.
- Letters of Paul: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon.
- Non-Pauline letters: Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude.
- Apocalyptic: Revelation.
These are the 73 books of the Catholic canon.

The Protestant Bible has 66 books. The books removed by Martin Luther after the Protestant Reformation are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees. They also removed chapters 10 to 16 of Esther and these sections of Daniel: Daniel 3:24-90, and chapters 13 and 14.

(Luther first moved these books into a separate section at the back of his Bible; later Protestant Bibles left them out. Catholics call them the deuterocanonical books. They were in the Greek Old Testament the early Christians used, and the Church has always counted them as Scripture.)
## How do we start studying the Bible and praying with God's Word?
- The Church has always seen the Scriptures as essential to nourish and guide Christian lives (Catechism 131).
- Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ. (St. Jerome, quoted in Catechism 133)

> The Holy Bible is like a mirror before our mind's eye. In it we see our inner face. From the Scriptures we can learn our spiritual deformities and beauties. And there too we discover the progress we are making and how far we are from perfection. — Pope St. Gregory the Great

1. We listen to the Word of God at every Mass. One way to start reading Scripture is to read the readings before every Sunday. There are wonderful missals that give you the daily Mass readings along with meditations and prayers. Some of the best are The Word Among Us and The Magnificat, which has its own app (make sure to get the English version, not the US version).

2. Use Scripture during your daily prayer time. You could begin by reading one of the Gospels, a chapter or even a few verses every day. The book of Psalms is also great for meditation. They are the prayers of King David, in both good and bad times.

3. God speaks to you personally through Scripture. Even one simple line can bring great insight or comfort. The Word of God is for everyone, so don't worry about how much you understand or already know. Don't be intimidated, just begin!

Your sheet also quotes Mother Angelica, the American nun who founded EWTN, from her book Private and Pithy Lessons From the Scriptures. In my own words, she says: we often treat the Gospel as a record of Jesus' life, something locked in the past, almost a divine history book. In a way it is, because it is the story of salvation history. But it is much more than that: it is a guide for living. Her approach to Scripture was spiritual. She tried to apply what she read to everyday life, because it is the truth. So you can't just read it like any other book.
## For further reflection and study: covenants

All through the Old Testament, God made a series of covenants with the Israelites, his chosen people. They began with Adam and continued all the way to King David, until the covenant was fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
What is a covenant? Your sheet explains it with Dr. Scott Hahn's book A Father Who Keeps His Promises (pages 24-27). In my own words:
- Coming together: the word means to come together, or to agree. A covenant is a formal, solemn and binding pact between two or more parties, and each one must keep its side.
- More than a contract: an earthly contract exchanges property and is sealed with a promise. A covenant exchanges persons and is sealed with a solemn oath.
- An oath: when you swear an oath you call on God's name, so you place yourself under God's judgment and accept a curse on yourself if you break it. The oath is the foundation of the covenant.

- Family bonds: Scripture shows how God has used covenants in every age to make his people his family. So to get to the heart of Scripture, Hahn says, think covenant, not contract; father, not judge; family room, not courtroom.

In the Old Testament we see a long line of covenants being made and then broken by the disobedience and sinfulness of the Israelites. Because they had sworn oaths, breaking the covenants brought a curse upon them.

In the New Testament, Jesus establishes the new covenant. He fulfills the covenant, even taking on himself all the curses of humanity's broken promises. Now he is the only mediator between God the Father and mankind.
[[figure:covenants]]

deeper.title: The new covenant at every Mass
deeper.text: At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you" (Luke 22:20, Douay-Rheims). "Testament" here means covenant. That is why the sign of the new covenant on your chart is the Eucharist: every Mass renews it.

sessions.title: The story of salvation: creation, fall, and redemption
sessions.summary: The whole Bible in three words: Creation, Fall, Redemption. God made us one family, sin broke it, and Jesus gathers us home.

sources.title: Genesis 12:1-3 and 22:15-18: God's promises to Abraham
Pope Benedict XVI, homily at the start of his pontificate (2005)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 4
lesson: [[art:Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg|Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam (about 1512), Sistine Chapel, Vatican]]
The three major parts of the Story of Salvation are Creation, Fall and Redemption.

Your workbook calls this, like the famous film, "the greatest story ever told," and it is the story we profess in the Creed. In my own words, its point is this: the story gives our lives a purpose. We are not just spectators watching time go by. From the moment our first parents rebelled against God, through the death and resurrection of his Son, Jesus, God has been writing his plan of salvation. Each of us has a God-given part to play in it. If we refuse God's loving invitation, the whole world is poorer, because God's story of love is not complete without each one of us.
## Creation
When God created man and woman, he created them to know and love him. In the beginning, humanity lived in perfect harmony with God and with each other.
## Fall

Adam and Eve disobeyed God and ate from the tree of knowledge. It was a refusal to give themselves in love. This "original sin" broke not only our harmony with God but also the harmony within humanity, and it left us with an inclination toward sin, called concupiscence.
- Original sin: not a sin we committed ourselves, but a wounded human nature we inherit (Catechism 404-405).
- Concupiscence: the pull toward sin that stays even after Baptism. It is not a sin in itself, but it makes the good harder to choose (Catechism 405, 1264).
## Redemption

God sent his Son Jesus to die for our sins and to offer the perfect gift of love that restores us to the Father. And he sent the Holy Spirit to fill us with his very life. The Catholic Church passes on Christ's teaching and, through the sacraments, gives us the graces he won for us on the Cross.
## Your drawing of the story
[[figure:salvation]]
- Creation: Adam and Eve. Unity in the human family: a united family.
- Fall: sin. It hurt our relationship with God and with each other, both the vertical and the horizontal: a broken human family. The harmony between man and woman was broken.
- God's plan: God had a plan to restore humanity to himself and to each other through certain leaders.
- Redemption: Jesus restores us to the Father and to each other: one family of God. Jesus pays the debt of sin and opens the door to eternal life.
[[figure:ladder]]

Step by step, through Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses and David, God's family grew: a couple, one family, one tribe, one nation, one kingdom. At the top stands the Cross, and the one universal Catholic Church.
## God's three promises to Abraham
1. Nation: that his descendants would be a great nation. This was fulfilled when Moses freed the Israelites from slavery under the Egyptians.
2. Kingdom: fulfilled when King David expanded Israel's borders and it became a kingdom.
3. Worldwide blessing: Abraham was told that God would send the Messiah to gather all the nations back. This was fulfilled in Jesus, as the new and everlasting covenant.
## The Catholic Church (the renewed family of God) is to:
1. Proclaim the Gospel.
2. Baptize.
3. Make disciples of all humanity.
After Jesus ascended into heaven, the apostles continued to do these three things. This will continue until the end of time, when Jesus will come back to judge the living and the dead.
Jesus didn't come to save us individually. He established the universal Catholic Church to gather the broken family of man into the united family of God.
## Key points from the workbook
- Made to share his goodness: God, perfect and happy in himself, freely created us to share in his own goodness and love (Catechism 1).

- Two kinds of harmony: at first we were united with God (the vertical level) and lived in harmony as one human family (the horizontal level). Humanity was God's united family, reflecting the unity of God himself (Catechism 376).
- The first sin: man and woman disobeyed God and refused to give themselves in love (Catechism 397-398).
- What it broke: that sin broke our relationship with God and the harmony between man and woman (Catechism 396).
- What it left: original sin brought death into the world and wounded our human nature, leaving us inclined toward sin, which is called concupiscence (Catechism 400, 404-405).

- Christ's gift: God sent his Son to die for our sins, offering for us the perfect gift of love that restores us to the Father, and to send the Holy Spirit to fill us with his life (Catechism 457-460).
- One family again: Jesus founded the universal, "catholic," Church to gather the broken human family into the united family of God (Catechism 830).

- The Church's work: the Church passes on Christ's teaching and, through the sacraments, gives the graces he won on the Cross, so that we can live like Christ on earth and with him forever in heaven (Catechism 774-776, 849).
## How do we live this story in our individual lives?
We all have a part to play in God's plan for salvation.
> Each of us is the result of a thought of God. Each of us is willed, each of us is loved, each of us is necessary. — Pope Benedict XVI

We are called to choose between good and evil in the world today. Jesus calls us toward his love and a life lived in virtue. He wants each of us to be part of spreading his love to everyone we meet. Satan is the chief enemy of all that is good, inviting people to live for the world and a life of sin. He distracts us from the true meaning of life through busyness and amusements. You either walk towards the light of Christ, or towards the darkness and despair of the evil one.

deeper.title: Why the story matters
deeper.text:
Without Creation, we would not know we are loved and made on purpose. Without the Fall, we could not explain why the world, and our own hearts, are so mixed up. Without Redemption, there would be no hope.

People sometimes call the Bible's story the greatest story ever told. It is better than a story, because it is true: God wrote himself into history to bring his children home.

- Catholic: from the Greek kath' holou, "according to the whole": the Church is for every people, place and time (Catechism 830-831).

- Redemption: buying back. Jesus paid the price of our freedom with his own life (Mark 10:45).

sessions.reflection: Where do you see the "broken lines" in your own life, with God or with the people around you? What is one small step toward the light this week?

sessions.title: Who is Jesus?
sessions.summary: Jesus is truly God and truly man: one divine Person with two natures. The Church guarded this truth against every distortion, because our salvation depends on it.

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 5
lesson: > It is Jesus that you seek when you dream of happiness; he is waiting for you when nothing else you find satisfies you; he is the beauty to which you are so attracted; it is he who provokes you with that thirst for fullness that will not let you settle for compromise; it is he who urges you to shed the masks of a false life; it is he who reads in your heart your most genuine choices, the choices that others try to stifle. — Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day, Rome, August 19, 2000
[[art:Spas vsederzhitel sinay.jpg|Christ Pantocrator (6th century), St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai: one face, truly God and truly man]]
## Christ Jesus: Mediator and fullness of all Revelation
God has said everything in his Word.

> "In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son." Christ, the Son of God made man, is the Father's one, perfect and unsurpassable Word. In him he has said everything; there will be no other word than this one. — Catechism 65

St. John of the Cross explained this beautifully: in giving us his Son, his only Word, God spoke everything to us at once, and he has nothing more to say. What he spoke to the prophets in parts, he has now spoken all at once by giving us his Son. So anyone who still asks God for some new vision or revelation would be offending him, by not fixing their eyes entirely on Christ and by looking for something new (Catechism 65).
There will be no further Revelation.

> The Christian economy, therefore, since it is the new and definitive Covenant, will never pass away; and no new public revelation is to be expected before the glorious manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet even if Revelation is already complete, it has not been made completely explicit; it remains for Christian faith gradually to grasp its full significance over the course of the centuries. — Catechism 66

Over the centuries there have been so-called "private" revelations, some of them recognized by the Church, like Lourdes or Fatima. They do not belong to the deposit of faith. Their role is not to improve or complete Christ's Revelation, but to help people live it more fully in a certain period of history. Guided by the Magisterium, the faithful can recognize which of them are a true call of Christ or his saints to the Church (Catechism 67).

God "desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4), that is, of Christ Jesus. So Christ must be proclaimed to all nations and all people, so that this revelation reaches the ends of the earth. God made sure that what he revealed for the salvation of all peoples would stay whole and be handed on to every generation (Catechism 74).
## True God and true man
Throughout early Church history, Christians worked to protect and explain the core truth of the Incarnation: that Jesus Christ is one divine Person, truly God and truly man.
- 479: At the time God chose, the only Son of the Father, the eternal Word, became incarnate. Without losing his divine nature, he took on a human nature.
- 480: Jesus Christ is true God and true man, in the unity of his divine Person. That is why he is the one and only mediator between God and men.
- 481: Jesus Christ has two natures, one divine and one human, not mixed together, but united in the one Person of God's Son.
- 482: Being true God and true man, Christ has a human mind and will, perfectly in tune with and obedient to his divine mind and will, which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit.
- 483: The Incarnation is the mystery of the wonderful union of the divine and human natures in the one Person of the Word.
[[figure:natures]]
## Errors about Jesus: the heresies
When people tried to understand these mysteries, they often fell into errors, called heresies. They either distorted his human nature or distorted his divine nature.
## Heresies that denied or shrank Jesus' divine nature

- Arianism (4th century): spread by Arius. It taught that the Son of God was not eternal, but a created being: the highest and first of God's creatures, but not God himself. The Church condemned it at the first ecumenical Council, Nicaea (325 AD), confessing that the Son is "begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" (Catechism 465).
- Adoptionism (3rd century): claimed that Jesus was born purely human, and that God "adopted" him as his Son at his baptism or resurrection because he was so holy and obedient.
## Heresies that denied or shrank Jesus' human nature

- Docetism and Gnosticism (1st and 2nd centuries): from the Greek word dokein, "to seem" or "to appear." Docetists taught that Jesus was purely divine and only appeared to have a body, to eat, to suffer and to die on the Cross. Gnostics believed physical matter was evil, so they rejected the idea that God could take on real flesh (Catechism 465).

- Apollinarianism (4th century): held that Jesus had a real human body and soul, but no rational human mind; the divine Word took its place. The Church rejected it, because a human being without a human mind is not fully human.

- Monophysitism (5th century): claimed that after the Incarnation, Christ's human nature was completely absorbed into his divine nature. The Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) rejected it, affirming that Christ has two complete natures, divine and human, without confusion or change.
## Heresies that distorted the union of both natures

- Nestorianism (5th century): spread by Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople. It taught that Jesus was really two separate persons, a human person and a divine person, joined only by love or purpose. Nestorius refused to call Mary the Theotokos (Mother of God), saying she was only the mother of the human person. The Council of Ephesus (431 AD) condemned this, declaring that the divine Word united a human nature to himself in his one divine Person, which makes Mary truly the Mother of God (Catechism 466).
## Why it matters

The truth of who Jesus is is tied to our salvation. That is why the Church still fights false teachings today. If Jesus is not fully God, he does not have the power to forgive sins, defeat death and restore the union of humanity with God. If he is not fully man, he cannot fully enter our human condition, including suffering on our behalf, in order to heal and restore our human nature. The early Church Fathers said it this way: "What was not assumed by Christ was not redeemed."
## Lord, or not a good teacher at all

C.S. Lewis was an Oxford professor, a famous 20th-century defender of the Christian faith, and the author of The Chronicles of Narnia. Your sheet quotes his best-known argument. In my own words: people often say, "I accept Jesus as a great moral teacher, but not his claim to be God." That is the one thing we must not say. A man who said the things Jesus said, if he were only a man, would not be a great teacher. He would be either a madman or something far worse. You have to choose: either he was, and is, the Son of God, or he was a lunatic or a liar. You can reject him, or you can fall at his feet and call him Lord and God. But he did not leave open the option of calling him just a good human teacher, and he did not mean to.
## Meeting him in prayer

Your sheet also quotes Bishop Fulton J. Sheen, who made a Holy Hour before the Blessed Sacrament every day. In my own words: neither knowing theology nor doing good works is enough, on its own, to keep us in love with Christ. Both must come from a personal meeting with him. We learn about God not only from the pages of a book, but on our knees before the altar. Sheen said the Holy Hour was like an oxygen tank for his soul, bringing back the breath of the Holy Spirit in the middle of a polluted world.
> Jesus saith to him: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No man cometh to the Father, but by me. — John 14:6, Douay-Rheims

deeper.title: Words the Church uses for Jesus
deeper.text:
- Incarnation: from the Latin for "in the flesh." The Son of God became man in the womb of the Virgin Mary (John 1:14).

- Hypostatic union: the theologian's name for two natures united in one divine Person.

- Consubstantial: of the same substance. We say it in the Creed: the Son is God in exactly the same way the Father is.

- Theotokos: Greek for God-bearer. Calling Mary the Mother of God is really a statement about who Jesus is.

- Christ: Greek for Messiah, "the anointed one." It is a title, not a surname.

sessions.reflection: Jesus asks you, not just the apostles: "Who do you say that I am?" How would you answer today? Try spending fifteen quiet minutes with him this week, in a church if you can.

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 6
lesson: The Paschal Mystery is the mystery of Jesus' death and resurrection.
[[art:Cristo crucificado.jpg|Diego Velázquez, Christ Crucified (about 1632), Prado Museum, Madrid: the painting on your Lesson 6 sheet]]
## The Cross was shocking

Your sheet quotes the Symbolon workbook (page 70). In my own words: the Cross may have become too familiar to us, because we see crosses and crucifixes so often. In the ancient world it was a horrifying image. A Roman wearing a cross around his neck as jewelry would be like one of us wearing a little electric chair: not just strange, but shocking. Yet the Cross is the main symbol of our faith, because it was through Jesus' death on that instrument of torture that he gave us salvation and eternal life.

We call Jesus' work of redemption, done above all through his Passion, Death, Resurrection and Ascension into heaven, the Paschal Mystery. "Paschal" means Jesus offered his life as the new Passover (Paschal) Lamb for our salvation. We say it at every Mass: "We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again."

Underneath it all is one simple reality: Jesus gives himself completely, in love, to the Father on our behalf, to restore our relationship with God. And by his death on the Cross, Jesus also shows us that we are called to the same self-giving love, which leads to true happiness on earth and eternal joy in the next life.
## Why did Jesus die for our sins?
1. A gap between God and humanity: because of sin there was a true break between God the Father and man.
2. We cannot overcome this gap on our own: it is not humanly possible to bridge it. Only a divine, supernatural act could do it. It needed something of infinite worth.

3. God becomes man to overcome sin: Jesus became the living sacrifice that was foreshadowed in the Old Testament. He took on all our sins, freely, to free us from sin. Because Jesus was both human and divine, he was able to do this.
[[figure:bridge]]
## Jesus descended to the dead

> When Jesus "descended into hell" in the Creed, this does not refer to the place of damnation, but the realm of the dead. Jesus in his human soul united to his divine person went to the realm of the dead and opened heaven's gates for the just who had gone before him. — Catechism 637 (as summarized on your sheet)

The place where Jesus went down was called Sheol in Hebrew and Hades in Greek. Jesus went there because the people there were deprived of the vision of God. That was true of all the dead, whether evil or good, while they waited for the Messiah. Jesus did not go down to free the damned, or to destroy the hell of damnation, but to free the just who had gone before him.

This descent brings the Gospel message of salvation to its complete fulfillment. It is the last phase of Jesus' messianic mission: short in time, but huge in meaning. It spreads Christ's saving work to all people of all times and all places. Everyone, from the creation of man to the end of time, is brought into this redemption (Catechism 633-634).
## Jesus rose from the dead
> By his death, Christ liberates us from sin; by his Resurrection, he opens for us the way to a new life. — Catechism 654
The Catechism goes on: this new life makes us sons and daughters of God, so that we may have eternal life.
Jesus has raised us up in a new life! He also opened the doors to heaven, which is eternal life with God and with all those who have gone before us.
## Jesus invites us to share in the mystery of his death and resurrection
Jesus invites us to share in the mystery of his Death and Resurrection by uniting our whole lives (our daily work, our joys and our sufferings) with the Cross of Christ (Catechism 618).
The Cross and Resurrection are the central points in history. They are also the central point in all of our lives.
We will all suffer in some way during our lives. This cannot be avoided. So the question should not be "Will I suffer?" but rather "What will I do when I suffer?"
## True love is always sacrificial
- True love is sacrificial, selfless, and always focused on God and others.
- When you live only for yourself, you become selfish, denying your own mortality and your true purpose.
- Our sufferings are an opportunity to unite ourselves with the suffering of Jesus.
## A prayer to Christ Crucified

Your sheet ends with a prayer attributed to St. Thérèse of Lisieux. In my own words, it goes like this: I come before you with empty hands, because I have given away every bit of grace to hearts in need, crying out in the dark night of fear and loneliness. You were so generous with your love. I keep your empty hands in front of me, emptied and torn by the nails, pouring out rivers of mercy until you had given everything. So I, my Jesus, with hands emptied for love of you, stand with confidence before your Cross, the crimson sign of love. It is the empty who are filled: those who give themselves away for you alone, and care for the least of your brothers and sisters, are nourished by your love. They are emptied more and more so that they may be filled with you.
Pray it slowly in front of a crucifix, and use the words from your class sheet if you have it with you.

deeper.title: The Triduum: three days at the heart of the year
deeper.text:
The Paschal Mystery is celebrated every Sunday, and above all in the Easter Triduum, the three holiest days of the Church year.

- Holy Thursday: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, when Jesus gives us the Eucharist and the priesthood, and washes his disciples' feet.

- Good Friday: the Celebration of the Lord's Passion. There is no Mass; we venerate the cross.

- Holy Saturday and the Easter Vigil: the Church waits at the tomb, then lights the new fire and sings the Exsultet. At the Vigil, those finishing RCIA are baptized, confirmed and receive their First Communion.

The Paschal Mystery is where your own journey is heading.
